cards.explanation: The answer is rash. Job says his grief would outweigh the sand of the seas, so no wonder his words have been rash. I think he's telling his friends where those words are coming from. A man carrying that much doesn't talk like somebody reading a recipe out loud.

The answer is the Almighty's. Job says, “…the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me…” and he adds that the terrors of God are arrayed against him. That's how Job describes it, and he says it out loud to his friends. It's a heavy way to talk, and I think it shows how deep the hurt goes.

The answer is True. Job says, “My soul refuses to touch them; they are loathsome food to me.” He doesn't hold back one bit, friends. I'd say a man who calls something loathsome food has made up his mind about it.

The answer is that he hopes God will crush him and cut him off. Job says, “…that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!” I think this one hurts. It's a heavy thing to hear a man hope for, and I'd rather sit quietly with it than try to be clever.

The answer is that he never denied God's words. Job says it still brings him comfort, “…and joy through unrelenting pain, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.” Look at that, friends. Right in the middle of all that pain, he finds one thing to hold onto, and I think that's worth noticing.

The answer is False, because Job asks it as a question. He says, “Is my strength like that of stone, or my flesh made of bronze?” I think the answer he's driving at is no. Nobody here is made of bronze, and Job knows it better than most.

The answer is False. Job asks, “Is there any help within me now that success is driven from me?” It's a question, and I think the answer he has in mind is no. That's a long way from plenty, friends, and I bet he feels emptied out.

The answer is kindness. Job says, “A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.” It's a simple thing to ask. A friend who shows up with a plate of cookies and no lecture is doing it right.

The answer is that they vanish from their channels. Job says the wadis cease in the dry season, “…vanishing from their channels in the heat.” They look great when the snow melts, and then the heat shows up and they're gone. Job says his brothers are as faithless as those streams.

The answer is Tema and Sheba. Job says, “The caravans of Tema look for water; the travelers of Sheba hope to find it.” Tema and Sheba are where those caravans and travelers come from. They went looking for water, and they hoped, friends. That hope is what makes the next verse sting.

The answer is True. Job says it straight to his friends: “you see terror, and you are afraid.” He starts with “For now you are of no help…” That's a hard thing to hear from a friend, and he says it anyway.
The answer is False. Job asks, “Have I ever said, ‘Give me something; offer me a bribe from your wealth…’” I think he means he never said it. It's a question, so that's my read of it.

The answer is how he has erred. Job says, “Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred.” He's asking to be shown, and he says he'll listen if they do. That's a pretty open-handed offer, friends.

The answer is his cry of despair. Job asks, “Do you intend to correct my words, and treat as wind my cry of despair?” A cry of despair isn't a speech to be graded. I think he wants his friends to hear the cry first.

The answer is righteousness. Job says, “Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake.” He says reconsider twice, so he really means it. I think he wants his friends to look at him again.

The answer is False. Job asks, “Is there iniquity on my tongue? Can my mouth not discern malice?” They're questions, so this is my read: no iniquity on his tongue, and yes, his mouth can discern malice. He finishes his plea standing by his words.

The answer is False. Job says, “So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed to me.” That's about his own months and nights. Rest and peace aren't anywhere in that sentence, friends.

The answer is that he tosses and turns. Job says the night drags on, “…and I toss and turn until dawn.” He lies down wondering when he'll get up, and the night just keeps going. Anybody who's watched the clock all night knows that one.

The answer is hope. Job says, “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle; they come to an end without hope.” A weaver's shuttle zips back and forth really fast. That's how quickly he feels his days are passing.

The answer is False, friends. Job says, “Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness.” (Job 7:7) He doesn't say happiness is coming back. I think this is a sad moment, and I'd rather sit with it than hurry past it.

The answer is that it remembers him no more. Job says, “He never returns to his house; his place remembers him no more.” He's describing the one who goes down to Sheol. It's a lonely picture, and Job doesn't dress it up.

The answer is False. Job says, “Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.” He isn't holding his mouth back, friends. He's going to speak and he's going to complain.

The answer is that God must keep him under guard. Job asks God, “Am I the sea, or the monster of the deep, that You must keep me under guard?” He's asking why God watches him so closely. It's a question, and Job brings it straight to God.

The answer is True. Job says, “…so that I would prefer strangling and death over my life in this body.” This is a heavy verse, and I think it hurts to read. Job isn't hiding it, friends, and I'd say that honesty matters.

The answer is whether God will ever look away. Job asks, “Will You never look away from me, or leave me alone to swallow my spittle?” He's asking God directly. I think he sounds worn out by the long nights he just described.

The answer is his target. Job asks, “Why have You made me Your target, so that I am a burden to You?” Before that, he says, “If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind?” He's bringing it right to God, friends, and I think that's an honest way to pray.
The answer is True. Job asks, “Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity?” He's bringing the question to God and not to his friends. Job asks it plainly.
